screens.title: Advanced Web Interaction
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn the practical tools and safe habits for interacting with web services using Python. We focus on three pillars: authenticating to APIs, maintaining stateful sessions across requests, and scraping public pages responsibly. You will see concrete examples using token-based authentication and the requests. Session object, and we’ll ground scraping best practices with a simple BeautifulSoup walkthrough. These skills matter because production services require both security and reliability: tokens avoid sending credentials repeatedly, sessions preserve cookies and user state, and respectful scraping prevents service disruption and legal issues. A short contrast helps orientation: Basic authentication sends credential pairs directly and is easy but risky over plain HTTP, while token-based flows avoid repeated credential exchange and enable revocation. OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework you’ll recognize conceptually for third-party access. By the end of this module you will know how to authenticate, persist state, and scrape with etiquette — and you’ll be able to handle rate limits and common network errors. Think about a task you might automate and whether it needs a token, a session, or simply a respectful scraper.

screens.title: Authentication Patterns: Basic, Token, OAuth 2.0
screens.narratorSegment: Authentication determines how a client proves identity to a server. Basic authentication encodes a username and password in the Authorization header. It is straightforward and works for simple internal tools, but on insecure channels it exposes credentials; always prefer HTTPS if you must use it. Token-based authentication separates credentials from session tokens: you provide credentials once, receive a token, and then send that token on subsequent requests, typically as Authorization: Bearer token. This reduces repeated credential exposure and allows the server to revoke tokens. OAuth 2.0 is a broader authorization framework used when third-party access is needed. It delegates permission from the resource owner to the client and issues limited-scope tokens. In Python client code you commonly use a library to handle the OAuth dance; understanding that OAuth focuses on authorization — what the application can do — helps avoid confusion with authentication, which answers who the user is. Concrete example: an A P I that issues an A P I key after signup — you store that key and send it each request in an Authorization header. Common misconception: thinking OAuth always authenticates the user. Instead, OAuth grants scoped access, and user identity is typically provided by an additional identity token or separate auth step. Key takeaway: match the method to your risk model: Basic for simple, internal use over HTTPS; token-based for APIs; OAuth for delegated third-party access.

keyIdea.title: Choose Wisely
keyIdea.text: Basic is simple, tokens scale better, OAuth is for delegated, third-party authorization.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.9 › Authentication Patterns
Definition

Basic, Token, and OAuth 2.0

Each method defines how credentials or tokens are exchanged and validated. Consider security, revocation, and delegation when selecting one.

Basic Authentication
Credentials are base64-encoded and sent per request. Use only over HTTPS and preferably for simple internal tooling.
Token-based Authentication
Server issues a token after initial login. Send the token as a Bearer in the Authorization header.
OAuth 2.0 (Conceptual)
An authorization framework for delegating limited access to third-party apps via scoped tokens.
Concrete example
import requests

API_KEY = "your_super_secret_api_key_here"
API_ENDPOINT = "https://api.example.com/data"

headers = {
  "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
  "Content-Type": "application/json"
}

response = requests.get(API_ENDPOINT, headers=headers)
response.raise_for_status()
print(response.json())
Misconception
OAuth is not just "login" — it grants limited access to resources and is about authorization, not simply authentication of a user.
Key Takeaway

Match the authentication method to your needs: risk, revocation, and third-party delegation drive the choice.

screens.title: Token Authentication in requests
screens.narratorSegment: Token authentication is one of the most common patterns you’ll use in A P I clients. The sequence is simple: obtain or provision a token, then send it in an Authorization header on each request. In Python we use requests. get or requests. post with a headers dictionary. The example demonstrates a bearer token sent in Authorization: Bearer token. Always call response. raise_for_status to convert 4xx and 5xx responses into exceptions you can handle. A concrete example from the chapter shows checking for HTTPError and RequestException separately so you can inspect a failed response body and respond appropriately. A common mistake is to ignore response. raise_for_status and assume. json will succeed; this can raise additional exceptions or give misleading data. Also avoid embedding long-lived tokens in source code; instead load them from secure storage or environment variables. In practice, if a server returns 401 you should refresh the token or prompt for re-authentication. If it returns 429 apply a retry with backoff. Hands-on: test against a mock endpoint that validates bearer tokens, and handle HTTP errors explicitly so your client behaves predictably. What will your client do if a token expires mid-session? Plan for refresh and graceful failure.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.9 › Token Authentication
Code Walkthrough
import requests

API_KEY = "your_super_secret_api_key_here"
API_ENDPOINT = "https://api.example.com/data"

headers = {
  "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
  "Content-Type": "application/json"
}

try:
  response = requests.get(API_ENDPOINT, headers=headers)
  response.raise_for_status()
  data = response.json()
  print("Data fetched successfully:", data)
except requests.exceptions.HTTPError as e:
  print(f"HTTP Error: {e}")
  print(f"Response content: {e.response.text}")
except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
  print(f"An error occurred: {e}")
This snippet shows header use and specific exception handling for HTTP errors and generic request failures.
Explanation
  • Place the token in Authorization to avoid re-sending credentials.
  • Call raise_for_status to detect 4xx/5xx and inspect the response for debug info.
  • On 401, refresh or re-authenticate; on 429, implement backoff before retrying.
Common Mistake

Hard-coding tokens in source makes leaks likely; use environment variables or secure vaults.

screens.title: requests.Session: Persisting State and Cookies
screens.narratorSegment: Many websites use cookies to maintain state. requests. Session gives you a simple client-side cookie jar and a place to set headers that persist across requests. Creating a Session is straightforward: you instantiate a Session object, optionally update its headers with a User-Agent or token, then use session. post or session. get for subsequent calls. The session object remembers cookies set by the server, so after logging in with session. post, later calls to protected endpoints will include those cookies automatically. This is essential when a site uses cookie-based login flows rather than token headers. A common mistake is using requests. get for each call and forgetting cookies will not persist, which leads to repeated redirects to login pages. Another useful pattern is adding default headers to session. headers so you avoid duplicating the same Authorization or User-Agent header on each call. Concrete example from the chapter logs into an example site then retrieves the dashboard content using the same Session. Inspect session. cookies. get_dict to verify the presence of cookies. Takeaway: use requests. Session whenever you need to simulate a browser-like, stateful interaction and to reduce code duplication of headers.

keyIdea.title: Session Value
keyIdea.text: Use requests.Session to persist cookies and headers so a client behaves like a continuous user session.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.9 › Session Management
How it works
A Session stores cookies and default headers. Use it to login once and perform many requests that share state.
import requests

s = requests.Session()
login_url = "https://example.com/login"
login_payload = {"username": "user", "password": "password"}
response_login = s.post(login_url, data=login_payload)
print(response_login.status_code)

protected = s.get("https://example.com/dashboard")
print(protected.status_code)
print(s.cookies.get_dict())
Notes & best practices
  • Attach shared headers to session.headers to avoid repetition.
  • Confirm cookies with session.cookies.get_dict during debugging.
  • Close sessions if long-lived resources are a concern: session.close().
Common mistake
Expecting cookies to persist across separate requests without a Session leads to authentication failures and redirects to login pages.
Key Takeaway

Use requests.Session to simulate user journeys and keep your client stateful and efficient.

screens.title: Session Example: Login and Protected Requests
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a full session example so you can see the pattern in practice. First, create a requests. Session and optionally set a User-Agent. Post credentials to the login endpoint with session. post. If login responds with a redirect or sets a cookie, the session captures it. Then use session. get to fetch protected pages. The chapter example prints the dashboard status and a snippet of H T M L to confirm access. Always call raise_for_status after each network call and inspect session. cookies. get_dict to make sure the login cookie exists. Real sites sometimes require CSRF tokens or additional hidden fields during login—if so you must fetch the login page first, parse the token, and include it in the post payload. A frequent misconception is assuming session. headers persist only for the first request; in fact, session. headers become defaults for all subsequent requests unless overridden. Finally, remember to close the session in long-running applications to free resources. This pattern reduces complexity in code and mirrors how browsers maintain user state during a browsing session. How will you check for CSRF tokens when a login fails?

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.9 › Session Login Example
Step-by-step
  1. Instantiate requests.Session and set headers.
  2. Fetch login page if CSRF tokens are required.
  3. Post credentials with session.post.
  4. Use session.get to access protected pages and verify cookies.
Live code (example)
import requests

s = requests.Session()
s.headers.update({"User-Agent": "CohortiaScraper/1.0"})

login_url = "https://example.com/login"
login_payload = {"username":"user","password":"pass"}
resp = s.post(login_url, data=login_payload)
resp.raise_for_status()
print("Login status:", resp.status_code)

dashboard = s.get("https://example.com/dashboard")
print("Dashboard status:", dashboard.status_code)
print(s.cookies.get_dict())
Use print statements to verify cookies or parse returned HTML for expected content.

screens.title: Web Scraping with requests and BeautifulSoup
screens.narratorSegment: Web scraping is the programmatic extraction of data from web pages. The minimal toolchain in Python is requests to fetch H T M L and BeautifulSoup to parse it. The typical flow is: check robots. txt and terms of service, set a descriptive User-Agent, wait a respectful delay, request the page, call raise_for_status, then create a BeautifulSoup object to find the elements you need. BeautifulSoup handles imperfect H T M L and provides simple methods to search by tag, id, class, or C S S selector. A concrete example from the chapter fetches a public Wikipedia page, finds the main content division, and extracts the first few paragraph elements. Common mistakes include scraping large portions of a site unnecessarily and ignoring rate limits which can lead to IP blocks. Another frequent problem is assuming page structure will remain stable—always code defensively by checking for None when using find or find_all. For static pages this pattern is robust; for dynamic pages you will need a headless browser or to discover the underlying A P I. Practice extracting a handful of links or the first paragraph text and include checks that abort gracefully if the expected tag is missing.

keyIdea.title: Scrape Pattern
keyIdea.text: Use requests to fetch HTML and BeautifulSoup to parse elements; always check robots.txt and handle missing elements gracefully.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.9 › requests + BeautifulSoup
Example code
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
import time

URL = "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Python_(programming_language)"
headers = {"User-Agent": "CohortiaAdvancedScraper/1.0 (contact@example.com)"}

time.sleep(2)
resp = requests.get(URL, headers=headers)
resp.raise_for_status()
soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.text, 'html.parser')
content_div = soup.find('div', class_='mw-parser-output')
if content_div:
  paragraphs = content_div.find_all('p')
  for p in paragraphs[:3]:
    print(p.text[:150])
Best practices
  • Respect robots.txt and Terms of Service before scraping.
  • Limit scope: scrape only the data you need.
  • Set a descriptive User-Agent and implement delays between requests.
  • Handle missing elements defensively to avoid crashes.
Pitfall

Scraping dynamically rendered content with only requests will miss post-load data; look for underlying APIs instead.

screens.title: Ethical Scraping: robots.txt, Rate Limits, and User-Agent
screens.narratorSegment: Ethical scraping is as much policy as it is code. The robots. txt file signals which parts of a site are off-limits to automated crawlers. Always check robots. txt before scraping and respect disallow rules. Next, rate limiting prevents server overload. If a server returns 429 Too Many Requests, pause and retry after a delay, ideally honoring the Retry-After header. Implementing fixed delays or exponential backoff helps you avoid triggering blocks. Set a clear User-Agent header that identifies your scraper and provides a contact — this increases trust and allows administrators to reach you if your scraper misbehaves. Another best practice is to scrape only what you need; avoid downloading large numbers of pages when you only need a few fields. Concrete example from the chapter: add time. sleep between requests and set a descriptive User-Agent string before fetching a Wikipedia page. A typical misconception is that robots. txt is legally binding; while it’s not a law everywhere, ignoring it invites blocking and possible legal risk when Terms of Service prohibit scraping. Key takeaway: be transparent and conservative — polite scrapers are less likely to be blocked and more likely to withstand production use.

Module 9 › Chapter 8.9 › Ethical Scraping
Policy Checklist
robots.txt
Check and follow directives for allowed paths.
Rate Limiting
Use delays and exponential backoff for 429 responses.
User-Agent
Identify your crawler with contact info to promote transparency.
Quick code hints
headers = {"User-Agent": "CohortiaAdvancedScraper/1.0 (contact@cohortia.com)"}
import time
# Respectful delay
for url in urls:
  time.sleep(2)
  resp = session.get(url, headers=headers)
  if resp.status_code == 429:
    # backoff logic here
    break
These minimal steps make your scraper less likely to trigger blocks and reduce the risk of harming the target site.

screens.title: Dynamic Content vs Static Pages
screens.narratorSegment: Not all web content is available in the initial H T M L document. Many sites load data via JavaScript after the page loads. requests and BeautifulSoup only see the initial H T M L payload, so they will miss post-load content. Before reaching for a headless browser, check the browser developer tools network tab to find if the page loads data from an A P I endpoint. If you can call that A P I directly, the result is typically more efficient and robust than simulating a browser. Use headless automation like Selenium or Playwright only when the data is generated on the client and no usable A P I exists. Headless browsers add complexity: they consume more resources, require managing a browser driver, and may be slower. A common misconception is that headless browsers are always more reliable; often they mask issues like brittle selectors and require additional handling for timeouts and dynamic waits. Practical strategy: try requests + BeautifulSoup first, then look for JSON endpoints the page calls, and only use a headless browser if those endpoints are not available. This approach saves resources and reduces fragility in scraping pipelines.

Before reaching for a headless browser, check the browser developer tools network tab to find if the page loads data from an A P I endpoint. If you can call that A P I directly, the result is typically more efficient and robust than simulating a browser. Use headless automation like Selenium or Playwright only when the data is generated on the client and no usable A P I exists. Headless browsers add complexity: they consume more resources, require managing a browser driver, and may be slower. A common misconception is that headless browsers are always more reliable; often they mask issues like brittle selectors and require additional handling for timeouts and dynamic waits. Practical strategy: try requests + BeautifulSoup first, then look for JSON endpoints the page calls, and only use a headless browser if those endpoints are not available. This approach saves resources and reduces fragility in scraping pipelines.

keyIdea.title: Choose Tools
keyIdea.text: Prefer API endpoints or requests + BeautifulSoup; use headless browsers only when necessary for dynamic, client-rendered content.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.9 › Dynamic vs Static
Static Pages
If the content you need is present in the initial HTML, requests + BeautifulSoup are efficient and robust. They avoid browser overhead and are simpler to maintain.
When to use requests
  • Page contains target data in HTML source.
  • There is an identifiable API endpoint returning JSON you can call directly.
Dynamic Pages
When data is rendered after page load via JavaScript, a headless browser can execute that script and provide the final DOM. Use this only when no direct API is available.
Trade-offs
  • Headless browsers are heavier, slower, and introduce more failure modes.
  • They can be necessary for single-page apps, but always check for underlying APIs first.

screens.title: Robust Error Handling and Retry with Backoff
screens.narratorSegment: Network calls fail for many reasons—transient server errors, rate limiting, or connectivity blips. To make clients robust, catch specific exceptions and design retries with exponential backoff. The chapter presents a make_robust_request function that retries on 429 and server errors like 503, doubling the wait time between attempts. The pattern is: try a request, on HTTP errors check status codes and decide whether to retry, compute the backoff wait time often as backoff_factor times two to the attempt number, and pause before the next attempt. Also catch RequestException to handle connection or timeout issues and retry as appropriate. Avoid retrying on client errors such as 400 or 401 unless you refresh credentials or tokens. Logging each attempt and eventual failure helps debugging. Concrete example: on a simulated 503 you retry a few times with increasing wait and then raise a RequestException if all retries fail. This approach reduces cascading failures in services and makes client code more tolerant of temporary outages. Ask: how many retries and what maximum wait time are acceptable for your application? Robust Error Handling and Retry with Backoff means retry on transient errors with exponential backoff; avoid retrying permanent client errors and log attempts for observability.. In practical terms, make network calls resilient to transient failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.9 › Retries & Backoff
make_robust_request
import requests
import time

def make_robust_request(url, headers=None, retries=3, backoff_factor=0.5):
  for i in range(retries):
    try:
      response = requests.get(url, headers=headers)
      response.raise_for_status()
      return response
    except requests.exceptions.HTTPError as e:
      if e.response.status_code == 429 or 503 <= e.response.status_code <= 504:
        wait_time = backoff_factor * (2 ** i)
        time.sleep(wait_time)
      else:
        raise
    except requests.exceptions.RequestException:
      time.sleep(backoff_factor * (2 ** i))
  raise requests.exceptions.RequestException("Failed after retries")
Notes
  • Retry only for transient, server-side conditions or rate limits.
  • Respect Retry-After headers when provided for polite behavior.
  • Log attempts and surface clear errors if retries ultimately fail.
Pro tip

Use a small max retry and sensible backoff to avoid amplifying load during outages.

screens.title: Assessment & Common Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Let's consolidate with an assessment mindset and review common pitfalls. The assessment idea in the chapter asks you to implement a client that uses an X-A P I-Key header, keeps a session, and handles 429 by retrying after a delay. The correct approach uses a requests. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn the practical tools and safe habits for interacting with web services using Python. We focus on three pillars: authenticating to APIs, maintaining stateful sessions across requests, and scraping public pages responsibly. You will see concrete examples using token-based authentication and the requests. Session object, and we’ll ground scraping best practices with a simple BeautifulSoup walkthrough. These skills matter because production services require both security and reliability: tokens avoid sending credentials repeatedly, sessions preserve cookies and user state, and respectful scraping prevents service disruption and legal issues. A short contrast helps orientation: Basic authentication sends credential pairs directly and is easy but risky over plain HTTP, while token-based flows avoid repeated credential exchange and enable revocation. OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework you’ll recognize conceptually for third-party access. By the end of this module you will know how to authenticate, persist state, and scrape with etiquette — and you’ll be able to handle rate limits and common network errors. Think about a task you might automate and whether it needs a token, a session, or simply a respectful scraper.

By the end of these slides you will be able to choose and implement appropriate authentication for APIs, use a requests. Session to maintain cookies and headers across a sequence of requests, and apply best practices for ethical and robust web scraping. Specifically, you will implement Basic and Token authentication patterns and recognize when OAuth 2.0 is required for third-party authorization. You will construct a session that preserves login cookies and persistent headers so an application can navigate a protected site without re-authenticating on every call. You will also design scrapers that respect robots. txt and rate limits, set a descriptive User-Agent, and include retry logic for transient errors. Each objective is framed as a practical competency: implement a bearer token header, use session cookies to access a protected page, and build a scraper that waits between requests and handles 429 responses. These skills matter in production: they improve security, reduce network overhead, and prevent service disruption. Consider which objective you most want to practice first and why.

This second objectives slide frames practice tasks and how they map to real code. You will write a small script that adds a bearer token to the Authorization header and observes the server response. You will use requests. Session to log in once and then visit protected pages without re-authenticating. You will create a minimal scraper that pauses between requests, sets a helpful User-Agent string, and parses H T M L with BeautifulSoup to extract specific elements. The lab requires you to simulate a 429 response and implement a retry with exponential backoff. These tasks matter because they convert conceptual security and respect into repeatable code patterns. Practicing them helps you avoid common mistakes like re-sending credentials on each request, forgetting to persist cookies, or overwhelming a server. During the live-coding demo you will use a mock A P I and a static public page so that you can focus on patterns instead of network variability. Pick one objective as your first lab target and plan a short test that verifies the behavior.

Authentication determines how a client proves identity to a server. Basic authentication encodes a username and password in the Authorization header. It is straightforward and works for simple internal tools, but on insecure channels it exposes credentials; always prefer HTTPS if you must use it. Token-based authentication separates credentials from session tokens: you provide credentials once, receive a token, and then send that token on subsequent requests, typically as Authorization: Bearer token. This reduces repeated credential exposure and allows the server to revoke tokens. OAuth 2.0 is a broader authorization framework used when third-party access is needed. It delegates permission from the resource owner to the client and issues limited-scope tokens. In Python client code you commonly use a library to handle the OAuth dance; understanding that OAuth focuses on authorization — what the application can do — helps avoid confusion with authentication, which answers who the user is. Concrete example: an A P I that issues an A P I key after signup — you store that key and send it each request in an Authorization header. Common misconception: thinking OAuth always authenticates the user. Instead, OAuth grants scoped access, and user identity is typically provided by an additional identity token or separate auth step. Key takeaway: match the method to your risk model: Basic for simple, internal use over HTTPS; token-based for APIs; OAuth for delegated third-party access.

Token authentication is one of the most common patterns you’ll use in A P I clients. The sequence is simple: obtain or provision a token, then send it in an Authorization header on each request. In Python we use requests. get or requests. post with a headers dictionary. The example demonstrates a bearer token sent in Authorization: Bearer token. Always call response. raise_for_status to convert 4xx and 5xx responses into exceptions you can handle. A concrete example from the chapter shows checking for HTTPError and RequestException separately so you can inspect a failed response body and respond appropriately. A common mistake is to ignore response. raise_for_status and assume. json will succeed; this can raise additional exceptions or give misleading data. Also avoid embedding long-lived tokens in source code; instead load them from secure storage or environment variables. In practice, if a server returns 401 you should refresh the token or prompt for re-authentication. If it returns 429 apply a retry with backoff. Hands-on: test against a mock endpoint that validates bearer tokens, and handle HTTP errors explicitly so your client behaves predictably. What will your client do if a token expires mid-session? Plan for refresh and graceful failure.

Many websites use cookies to maintain state. requests. Session gives you a simple client-side cookie jar and a place to set headers that persist across requests. Creating a Session is straightforward: you instantiate a Session object, optionally update its headers with a User-Agent or token, then use session. post or session. get for subsequent calls. The session object remembers cookies set by the server, so after logging in with session. post, later calls to protected endpoints will include those cookies automatically. This is essential when a site uses cookie-based login flows rather than token headers. A common mistake is using requests. get for each call and forgetting cookies will not persist, which leads to repeated redirects to login pages. Another useful pattern is adding default headers to session. headers so you avoid duplicating the same Authorization or User-Agent header on each call. Concrete example from the chapter logs into an example site then retrieves the dashboard content using the same Session. Inspect session. cookies. get_dict to verify the presence of cookies. Takeaway: use requests. Session whenever you need to simulate a browser-like, stateful interaction and to reduce code duplication of headers.

Let's walk through a full session example so you can see the pattern in practice. First, create a requests. Session and optionally set a User-Agent. Post credentials to the login endpoint with session. post. If login responds with a redirect or sets a cookie, the session captures it. Then use session. get to fetch protected pages. The chapter example prints the dashboard status and a snippet of H T M L to confirm access. Always call raise_for_status after each network call and inspect session. cookies. get_dict to make sure the login cookie exists. Real sites sometimes require CSRF tokens or additional hidden fields during login—if so you must fetch the login page first, parse the token, and include it in the post payload. A frequent misconception is assuming session. headers persist only for the first request; in fact, session. headers become defaults for all subsequent requests unless overridden. Finally, remember to close the session in long-running applications to free resources. This pattern reduces complexity in code and mirrors how browsers maintain user state during a browsing session. How will you check for CSRF tokens when a login fails?

Web scraping is the programmatic extraction of data from web pages. The minimal toolchain in Python is requests to fetch H T M L and BeautifulSoup to parse it. The typical flow is: check robots. txt and terms of service, set a descriptive User-Agent, wait a respectful delay, request the page, call raise_for_status, then create a BeautifulSoup object to find the elements you need. BeautifulSoup handles imperfect H T M L and provides simple methods to search by tag, id, class, or C S S selector. A concrete example from the chapter fetches a public Wikipedia page, finds the main content division, and extracts the first few paragraph elements. Common mistakes include scraping large portions of a site unnecessarily and ignoring rate limits which can lead to IP blocks. Another frequent problem is assuming page structure will remain stable—always code defensively by checking for None when using find or find_all. For static pages this pattern is robust; for dynamic pages you will need a headless browser or to discover the underlying A P I. Practice extracting a handful of links or the first paragraph text and include checks that abort gracefully if the expected tag is missing.

Ethical scraping is as much policy as it is code. The robots. txt file signals which parts of a site are off-limits to automated crawlers. Always check robots. txt before scraping and respect disallow rules. Next, rate limiting prevents server overload. If a server returns 429 Too Many Requests, pause and retry after a delay, ideally honoring the Retry-After header. Implementing fixed delays or exponential backoff helps you avoid triggering blocks. Set a clear User-Agent header that identifies your scraper and provides a contact — this increases trust and allows administrators to reach you if your scraper misbehaves. Another best practice is to scrape only what you need; avoid downloading large numbers of pages when you only need a few fields. Concrete example from the chapter: add time. sleep between requests and set a descriptive User-Agent string before fetching a Wikipedia page. A typical misconception is that robots. txt is legally binding; while it’s not a law everywhere, ignoring it invites blocking and possible legal risk when Terms of Service prohibit scraping.
